title: machinelogR
text: machinelogR turns any machine log into a standard event table. One format. One vocabulary. Every analysis on this site runs on it.

title: machinelogR
text:
The Lego principle
machinelogR is built like Lego.




A brick is a function. It does one thing: takes a standard input and returns a standard output.





flowchart LR
    A(["input"]) --> B["function()"]
    B --> C(["result"])







Bricks snap together into walls. A wall is a group of functions with a shared purpose.
Each step adds one layer of meaning. No step knows about the others. They just snap.

Walls can build houses. A house is a report: a CPV monitoring report, a maintenance prioritization dashboard, an audit trail review, etc.
And finally, houses form cities. There are two cities on this site:
 Part I: a pharmaceutical manufacturing site.
 Part II: an industrial production line.

title: machinelogR
text:
The pipeline
Every analysis follows the same path: raw data in, conclusions out.





flowchart TB
    subgraph etl["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/lucide:brick-wall.svg' width='14' height='14'/> Ingestion"]
        direction LR
        R[("raw export")] --> E["read_piade()"]
        E --> M["mlog()"]
        M --> L[("event log")]
    end
    subgraph ctrl["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/lucide:brick-wall.svg' width='14' height='14'/> Control chart"]
        direction LR
        B["spc_baseline()"] --> C["spc_chart()"]
    end
    etl --> B
    C --> P1(["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/mdi:hospital-building.svg' width='14' height='14'/> CPV report<br/>Part I"])
    C --> P2(["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/streamline-plump:factory-plant.svg' width='14' height='14'/> Maintenance dashboard<br/>Part II"])
    style etl fill:#f5f7fa,stroke:#b0bec5,color:#333
    style ctrl fill:#f5f7fa,stroke:#b0bec5,color:#333






Same bricks. Same walls. Two different cities.

mlog(): the contract
Every city needs a shared language.
In machinelogR, that language is mlog().
The raw data first goes through an ingestion step: an adapter function, specific to the data source (ex: Siemens PLC) that handles timestamps, column names, and encoding.
Then mlog() applies the contract. For example:
df <- mlog(raw_export,
           ts_col  = "timestamp", dir_col = "direction",
           on_val  = "ON", off_val = "OFF")
So, the output always has the same structure:
equipment_ID | type         | alarm | start (POSIXct) | end (POSIXct) | elapsed_s
-------------|--------------|-------|-----------------|---------------|----------
s_1          | production   |  -    | 2021-01-04 ...  | ...           | 3600
s_1          | downtime     | E042  | 2021-01-04 ...  | ...           | 245
type is a controlled vocabulary: “production”, “downtime”, “performance_loss”, “idle”, “scheduled_downtime”.
These five terms map directly to the OEE decomposition: the minimal set to compute Availability and Performance from any machine, regardless of how its native export labels the states.
The source equipment does not matter.
The column names of the raw file do not matter.
Once in this format, every downstream function works on it.

title: machinelogR
text:
ask()
A natural language interface sits on top of the modules.
A plain-text question. A structured answer. No knowledge of the underlying functions required.
And it speaks English and French.
ask(df, "which alarms caused the most downtime last month?")
ask(df, "show me the escalation pattern starting from E042")
ask() runs locally . No cloud.
And in a GxP context, every query and response could be logged automatically.
This is still a prototype, but it works.

title: machinelogR
text:
Two packages, not one
machinelogR handles discrete signals: alarms, intervals, event counts, state transitions.
A companion package, processlogR (in development), handles continuous signals: temperature curves, pressure profiles, sublimation rates.
Two grammars. Two packages. One shared design philosophy.

title: machinelogR
text:
Access
I built machinelogR for my own analytical work.
It is not on CRAN and not publicly hosted, but I’m happy to share the philosophy.

title: FDSim
text:
I wanted real and challenging data to test the functions I had built.
A freeze-dryer was the obvious choice: one of the most complex pieces of equipment I have worked with, but also one where open data is unavailable.
So I needed a simulator and I found one: LyoPRONTO, a Lyophilization Process Optimization Tool. Excellent. But written in Python, and designed to optimize the cycle, not to monitor the equipment.
I decided to build one, brick by brick. Not a small task.
Three things mattered:

Reproducibility : same inputs, same outputs, every time
Controlled faults : realistic failures, injected on demand
Open : nothing proprietary, nothing confidential

title: FDSim
text:
Physical basis





flowchart LR
    classDef hot  fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100,color:#333
    classDef warm fill:#fffde7,stroke:#f9a825,color:#333
    classDef cold fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,color:#333
    classDef pump fill:#f5f5f5,stroke:#9e9e9e,color:#333

    subgraph CH["<b>Chamber</b> · P_ch"]
        A["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/lucide:flame.svg' width='32' height='32'/><br/><b>Shelf</b><br/>T_shelf"]:::hot -->|heats| B["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/lucide:flask-conical.svg' width='32' height='32'/><br/><b>Product</b><br/>T_product"]:::warm
    end
    subgraph TR["<b>Cold trap</b> · P_ch"]
        D["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/lucide:snowflake.svg' width='32' height='32'/><br/><b>Condenser</b><br/>T_cond"]:::cold
    end
    B -->|water vapor| D
    D -->|maintains vacuum| E["<img src='https://api.iconify.design/material-symbols:water-pump-outline.svg' width='32' height='32'/><br/><b>Pump</b><br/>pump_load"]:::pump
    style CH fill:#f5f7fa,stroke:#b0bec5,color:#333
    style TR fill:#f5f7fa,stroke:#b0bec5,color:#333






Shelf to product : heat flows through the vial bottom. This energy feeds sublimation.
Product to chamber : ice sublimates into vapor, driven by the vacuum. The dried cake resists the flow as the lyophilization progresses.
Chamber to cold trap : water vapor is captured by the condenser. The pump maintains the vacuum that keeps the whole process running.








Signal simulated
Variable
What it represents




Shelf temperature
T_shelf
Heat delivered to the product


Product temperature
T_product
How cold the product still is


Chamber pressure
P_ch
Vacuum level driving sublimation


Condenser temperature
T_cond
Cold trap efficiency


Vacuum pump load
pump_load
Mechanical load on the vacuum system



 Each batch is a dataframe of timestamped readings.
Primary drying is the focus (where equipment monitoring matters most).







Phase / signal
Status




Primary drying
Benchmarked against LyoPRONTO: sublimation flux in close agreement


Freezing
Simulated, not benchmarked


Secondary drying
Out of scope: requires product-specific parameters not available from open data


Equipment signals
Phenomenological: plausible shapes, not benchmarked against real historian data

title: FDSim
text:
Almost a digital twin
FDSim is a generic model: the physics are fixed, the parameters are not.
calibrate() is the bridge: given real historian data, this function is designed to estimate the missing equipment-specific and product-specific parameters, and return a calibrated parameter set.
The rest of the chain (batch simulation, CPV charts, fault detection) remains unchanged.

title: The Ecosystem
text:
Two types of signals
Discrete events – alarms on/off, valve open/closed, operator entries…, timestamped.
This is what audit trails are made of. That’s what machinelogR reads.
Continuous measurements – temperature, pressure, weight… over time.
This is typically what historians store. That’s what processlogR will handle.
Different data. Same logic. Two sister packages.

title: The Ecosystem
text:
Architecture

A few examples of functions:
alarm_pareto() counts alarm frequencies.
spc_chart() plots a control chart.
lyo_batch() simulates a freeze-drying batch.
A function, a simulator, and a grammar rule are all bricks.
Bricks snap together into walls. Walls build houses – a CPV report, a maintenance dashboard, an audit trail review.

 →  → 
The same brick, like spc_chart(), may appear in different houses.
The context changes. The function does not.

title: The Ecosystem
text:
The datasets
All datasets used here are either open data or generated on this site.
PIADE (Packaging Industry Anomaly DEtection) is a real dataset – packaging line logs published as open data on Kaggle. That’s what I used to build and test machinelogR on actual industrial data.
FDSim is a freeze-dryer simulator I built for this site. You can explore it in the Toolbox.
IndPenSim (Industrial-scale Penicillin Simulation) is a public simulator for fed-batch bioreactors (industrialpenicillinsimulation.com). I use it to build and validate processlogR, and as a showcase for continuous bioprocess data.
Real data from real plants exists. It won’t appear here – but the tools are built to read it.
